'''''Rheum rhabarbarum''''' is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Polygonaceae]], native to a region stretching from southern [[Siberia]] to north and central China.<ref name=POWO_301818-2/> It has been harvested from the wild for centuries for its root, which was harvested for use as a popular medicine in Europe and Asia. It was later cultivated for its root in England and Russia. It is considered to be one of the species involved in the development of culinary [[rhubarb]], for which the scientific name ''R. rhabarbarum'' is sometimes (erroneously) used.

==Taxonomy==
''Rheum rhabarbarum'' was first described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753.<ref name=IPNI_301818-2/> Linnaeus also described ''R. undulatum'', but this is now considered to be the same species.<ref name=POWO_301818-2/>

The name ''rha barbarum'', [[Latin language|Latin]] for 'foreign rha', was first used in the writings of [[Celsus]], who uses the word to describe a valued medicinal root imported from the east.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Alam |first1=Shamshad |last2=Khan |first2=Naeem A. |date=2015 |title=Rhubarb (Rewand), A Review |url=https://applications.emro.who.int/imemrf/Hamdard_Med/Hamdard_Med_2015_58_1_84_95.pdf |journal=Hamdard Medicus |volume=58 |issue=1 |pages=84–96 |access-date=13 March 2019}}</ref>

==Description==
===Similar species===
According to the 2003 key in the ''[[Flora of China (series)|Flora of China]]'', this species is distinguished from other entire-leaved [[Rheum (plant)|rhubarbs]] in China with leaves having a wavy or crisped margin; [[Rheum wittrockii|''R. wittrockii'']], [[Rheum webbianum|''R. webbianum'']], [[Rheum australe|''R. australe'']] and [[Rheum hotaoense|''R. hotaoense'']], by having less than 1 cm-sized fruit, yellow-white to greenish-white flowers, and the surface of the rachis of [[panicle]] covered in [[wikt:papilla#English|papilla]]. In many characters it is most similar to ''R. webbianum'', and somewhat less so ''R. hotaoense''.<ref name=FlChina2>{{cite book |last1=Bojian (包伯坚) |first1=Bao |last2=Grabovskaya-Borodina |first2=Alisa E. |date=2003 |chapter=Rheum |chapter-url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=128294 |editor1-last=Zhengyi (吴征镒) |editor1-first=Wu |editor2-last=Raven |editor2-first=Peter H. |editor2-link=Peter H. Raven |editor3-last=Deyuan (洪德元) |editor3-first=Hong |title=Flora of China, Vol. 5 |url=http://www.efloras.org/flora_page.aspx?flora_id=2 |location=Beijing |publisher=Science Press |page=341 }}</ref>

===Karyotypy===
There have been at least two studies investigating the [[karyotype|karyotypy]] of this species, both studies focussing on the synonym ''R. undulatum''. Both 2''n''=22 and 2''n''=44 have been found. It is possible that this karyotypic diversity indicates the existence of one or more [[cryptic species]], because the [[polyploid]] forms would essentially be reproductively isolated.<ref name=karyotypes>{{cite journal |last1=Ruirui |first1=Liu |last2=Wang |first2=Ailan |last3=Tian |first3=Xinmin |last4=Wang |first4=Dongshi |last5=Liu |first5=Jianquan |date=2010 |title=Uniformity of karyotypes in Rheum (Polygonaceae), a species-rich genus in the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau and adjacent regions |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/261646487 |journal=Caryologia Firenze |volume=63 |issue=1 |pages=82–90 |doi=10.1080/00087114.2010.10589711 |s2cid=86616077 |access-date=24 March 2019|doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Distribution==
It is native to an area of southeastern [[Siberia]] in the [[Transbaikal|Daurian region]] around and stretching east from [[Lake Baikal]] in [[Russia]], and in northern [[Mongolia]].<ref name=AgroAtlas>{{cite web |url=https://www.agroatlas.ru/ru/content/related/Rheum_rhabarbarum/map/ |title=AgroAtlas - Дикие родичи культурных растений - Ареал Rheum rhabarbarum L. (Ревень волнистый) |last1=Смекалова |first1=Т.Н. |last2=Ушакова |first2=Р.С. |date=19 October 2004 |language=ru |website=AgroAtlas, Interactive Agricultural Ecological Atlas of Russia and Neighboring Countries |access-date=16 March 2019}}</ref><ref name=AgroAtlasEn>{{cite web |url=https://www.agroatlas.ru/en/content/related/Rheum_rhabarbarum/index.html |title=AgroAtlas - Relatives - Rheum rhabarbarum L. - Wavy Rhubarb |last=Smekalova |first=T.N. |website=AgroAtlas, Interactive Agricultural Ecological Atlas of Russia and Neighboring Countries |access-date=15 March 2019}}</ref> In China, it occurs in the northern provinces of [[Hebei]],<ref name=FlChina/><ref name=CatChina>{{cite web |url=http://www.chinaplantspecies.org/ |title=Species Catalogue of China, Plants |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=2017 |website=中国 生物物种名录 植物卷 |language=zh |location=Beijing |publisher=Science Press |access-date=15 March 2019 |archive-date=24 February 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190224062413/http://www.chinaplantspecies.org/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> [[Heilongjiang]],<ref name=FlChina/><ref name=CatChina/> [[Henan]],<ref name=CatChina/> [[Hubei]],<ref name=FlChina/><ref name=CatChina/> [[Jilin]],<ref name=FlChina/><ref name=CatChina/> [[Inner Mongolia]],<ref name=FlChina/><ref name=CatChina/> [[Shanxi]]<ref name=FlChina/><ref name=CatChina/> and [[Shaanxi]].<ref name=CatChina/>

[[File:Rheum undulatum - Bergianska trädgården - Stockholm, Sweden - DSC00564.JPG|thumb|''Rheum rhabarbarum'' growing in the [[Bergianska trädgården]] in [[Stockholm]], Sweden]]

==Habitat & ecology==
In China, it is known as a species growing on mountain slopes at 1,000–1,600 m elevation.<ref name=FlChina/> In Russia it occurs in sandy ground along field edges, on the steppes, and in the regionally uncommon copses of woodland.<ref name=AgroAtlas/>

In China, it flowers in June, and has fruit after July.<ref name=FlChina/>

Most documented insect relationships with this species are muddied by the misapplication of the name ''R. rhabarbarum'' to plants of ''R.'' × ''hybridum''. As such, most of the insects which are said to use this species as a food plant are generalists from Europe or North America which did not actually eat this species nor are native to the region where this species occurs. An exception is the butterfly ''[[Lycaena violacea]]'', whose caterpillars are only known to feed on ''R. rhabarbarum'' and whose range is concurrent with that of its host plant (most ''[[Lycaena]]'' spp. are specialised on [[Polygonaceae]]). ''[[Cosmia trapezina]]'' var. ''exigua'' is roughly native to some of the same areas, and its European variety has been found to have eaten rhubarb in Finland (it usually feeds on various tree species). Other species found to eat (garden) rhubarb which occur in the native range of this plant are ''[[Arctia caja]]'', ''[[Hydraecia micacea]]'', ''[[Spilarctia luteum]]'' and ''[[Xestia baja]]''.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://ftp.funet.fi/index/Tree_of_life/plants/magnoliophyta/magnoliophytina/magnoliopsida/polygonaceae/rheum/ |title=Rheum |last=Savela |first=Markku |date=27 September 1998 |website=Lepidoptera and some other life forms |publisher=Markku Savela |access-date=16 March 2019}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
''Rheum rhabarbarum'' (syn. ''R. undulatum'') was one of a number of distinct species grown in Europe before the beginning of the 18th century. Initially the roots of a related species, possibly ''[[Rheum rhaponticum|R. rhaponticum]]'', were used for medicinal purposes. A putative hybrid of unknown origin, [[Rheum × hybridum|''Rheum'' × ''hybridum'']], was also grown. The three taxa were grown as vegetable crops in England and Scandinavia by the early 18th century. They readily hybridize, and culinary [[rhubarb]] was developed by selecting open-pollinated seed, so that its precise origin is almost impossible to determine.<ref name=TanhSuojHart19/> In appearance, culinary rhubarb varies continuously between ''R. rhabarbarum'' and ''R. rhaponticum''. Modern rhubarb cultivars are [[tetraploid]]s with 2''n'' = 44, in contrast to 2''n''=22 for the wild species such as ''R. rhaponticum''.<ref name=LibeEngl89>{{Cite journal |last1=Libert |first1=Bo |last2=Englund |first2=Roger |date=1989 |title=Present Distribution and Ecology of ''Rheum rhaponticum'' (Polygonaceae) |journal=Willdenowia |volume=19 |issue=1 |pages=91–98 |jstor=3996925 |name-list-style=amp}}</ref>
